title: Jeremiah 39:1–10
context: Jeremiah 39:1–10 is told by the narrator and reports the fall of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar besieges the city from Zedekiah’s ninth year, tenth month, until a breach is made in the eleventh year, fourth month, ninth day (39:1–2). The parallel accounts in 2 Kings 25:1–12 and Jeremiah 52:4–16 add “in the tenth day of the month” for the start of the siege and tie the ninth day of the fourth month to the famine; these accounts are named here without harmonizing, and the conversion of these dates to modern calendars is discussed rather than settled. Babylonian officials sit in the middle gate (39:3). The names and titles are difficult: Rabsaris and Rabmag are generally taken as official titles rather than personal names, and readers differ on how to divide and identify the names, including whether one or two officials named Nergal Sharezer are meant. Zedekiah flees by night toward the Arabah and is overtaken in the plains of Jericho (39:4–5). At Riblah in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon passes judgment on him: his sons and the nobles of Judah are killed, his eyes are put out, and he is bound to be taken to Babylon (39:5–7). Jeremiah had warned Zedekiah that surrender would spare the city and his house (38:17–18), and earlier prophecies spoke of Zedekiah seeing the king of Babylon (32:4; 34:3) while Ezekiel says of the prince who is taken that “he will not see it, though he will die there” (Ezekiel 12:13); these are named without harmonizing. The city and houses are burned, the walls broken down, and Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carries the people into exile, leaving some of the poorest with vineyards and fields (39:8–10; compare 2 Kings 25:8–12, which places this in the fifth month on the seventh day, and Jeremiah 52:12–16, which gives the tenth day; the dates are named without harmonizing). Both traditions read these events with sober grief as the fulfillment of the LORD’s warnings, and questions about how God uses Babylon in judgment belong to the existing box at Judges 9:23 and are not reopened here.

verses.text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and all his army came against Jerusalem, and besieged it.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator dates the siege to Zedekiah’s ninth year, in the tenth month. Arminian readers note that the long siege followed many warnings, and they see in the precise date a sober marker of the moment when the LORD’s repeated calls to repent gave way to judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the parallel accounts in 2 Kings 25:1 and Jeremiah 52:4 add the tenth day of the month, named here without harmonizing. They read the dating as anchoring the fall of Jerusalem in real history, the moment when the LORD’s spoken word came to pass.

verses.text: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, the ninth day of the month, a breach was made in the city.
verses.arminianNotes: In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the ninth day, a breach was made in the city. Arminian readers note that the siege lasted well over a year, and they see the breach as the end of a long season in which the king could still have heeded Jeremiah’s counsel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 25:3–4 and Jeremiah 52:6–7 connect this date with severe famine, named without harmonizing. They read the breach as the fulfillment of what the LORD had announced, and they observe that the calendar details are discussed rather than settled by interpreters.

verses.text: All the princes of the king of Babylon came in, and sat in the middle gate: Nergal Sharezer, Samgarnebo, Sarsechim the Rabsaris, Nergal Sharezer the Rabmag, with all the rest of the princes of the king of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes of the king of Babylon sat in the middle gate, including Nergal Sharezer, Samgarnebo, and Sarsechim the Rabsaris. Arminian readers note that Rabsaris and Rabmag are generally taken as official titles, though how to divide and identify the names is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the identification of these officials loosely, including whether one or two men named Nergal Sharezer are in view. They observe that foreign officials sitting in the gate, the place of judgment and authority, marks the end of Judah’s independent rule.

verses.text: When Zedekiah the king of Judah and all the men of war saw them, then they fled and went out of the city by night, by the way of the king’s garden, through the gate between the two walls; and he went out toward the Arabah.
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah and the men of war fled by night through the gate between the two walls, and he went toward the Arabah. Arminian readers note that the king chose flight rather than the surrender Jeremiah had urged (38:17–18), and they see the consequences of refusing God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same refusal and observe that 2 Kings 25:4 and Jeremiah 52:7 describe the escape route in similar terms, named without harmonizing. They read the king’s flight as the fulfillment of warnings that he would not escape, and they read it with sober grief.

verses.text: But the army of the Chaldeans pursued them, and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. When they had taken him, they brought him up to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to Riblah in the land of Hamath; and he pronounced judgment on him.
verses.arminianNotes: The Chaldean army overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho and brought him to Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah in the land of Hamath, where judgment was pronounced on him. Arminian readers note that Riblah lay far to the north, and they see the king brought before the very power he had resisted.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the parallels in 2 Kings 25:5–6 and Jeremiah 52:8–9 give the same outline, named without harmonizing. They observe that Zedekiah’s capture echoes the prophecies that he would see the king of Babylon (32:4; 34:3), and they read the judgment soberly.

verses.text: Then the king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons in Riblah before his eyes. The king of Babylon also killed all the nobles of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons in Riblah before his eyes, and all the nobles of Judah. Arminian readers note the grief of a father and a nation at this loss, and they read the verse with pastoral sobriety, seeing the terrible cost when leaders refuse to heed God’s warnings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jeremiah 52:10 speaks of “all the princes of Judah in Riblah”, named without harmonizing. They read the verse soberly as part of the covenant judgment Jeremiah had announced, and they do not dwell on its horror beyond what the text records.

verses.text: Moreover he put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters, to carry him to Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: The king of Babylon put out Zedekiah’s eyes and bound him in fetters to carry him to Babylon. Arminian readers note that the king’s blinding may be read alongside 32:4 and 34:3, where he would see the king of Babylon, and Ezekiel 12:13, where he will not see Babylon, named without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same passages and observe that Jeremiah 52:11 adds that he was kept in prison “until the day of his death”. They read the verse with sober grief as the outcome of Zedekiah’s refusal to obey the word of the LORD, while not elaborating its cruelty.

verses.text: The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the people’s houses with fire and broke down the walls of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the people’s houses and broke down the walls of Jerusalem. Arminian readers note that the walls and houses that had seemed secure were destroyed, and they read the verse as the visible end of the city’s long resistance to God’s call to return.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 25:9 and Jeremiah 52:13 also mention the burning of the LORD’s house, named without harmonizing. They read the destruction as fulfilling the LORD’s word through Jeremiah, and both traditions grieve the loss while affirming God’s justice.

verses.text: Then Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried away captive into Babylon the rest of the people who remained in the city, the deserters also who fell away to him, and the rest of the people who remained.
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile the rest of the people in the city and the deserters. Arminian readers note that even those who went over to the Babylonians were carried away, and they see the exile as touching every group within the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallels in 2 Kings 25:11 and Jeremiah 52:15, named without harmonizing. They observe that Nebuzaradan’s title, captain of the guard, is generally understood as a high military office, and they read the deportation as the scattering the prophets had foretold.

verses.text: But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left of the poor of the people, who had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields at the same time.
verses.arminianNotes: Nebuzaradan left some of the poor of the people, who had nothing, in the land of Judah, and gave them vineyards and fields. Arminian readers note the reversal in which the poor receive land, and they see a glimmer of mercy within judgment that allowed life to continue in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal and the parallels in 2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16, named without harmonizing. They read the gift of vineyards and fields as showing that God’s judgment did not end his care for the land and the least of its people.
